text: Welcome to Quantum Hardware and Architectures. This first lesson starts at the physical foundation of superconducting quantum computing: how a tiny electrical circuit, etched on a chip, becomes a qubit.

A superconducting qubit isn't a trapped atom or a defect in a crystal — it's built out of ordinary circuit elements: capacitors, inductors, and one special nonlinear part, fabricated with the same lithography used for classical chips. Cooled below about one Kelvin, the wiring becomes a superconductor, and current flows as a coherent quantum wave instead of a noisy classical signal. The key ingredient is the Josephson junction: two superconducting electrodes separated by a few nanometers of insulator, thin enough for Cooper pairs of electrons to tunnel through. That junction behaves like a nonlinear inductor, and that nonlinearity produces anharmonicity — uneven spacing between energy levels — which is what lets engineers carve a clean two-level qubit out of a circuit that actually has many more levels above it. Once that two-level system exists, it's driven and read out with microwave photons, typically a few gigahertz, sent down a coaxial line onto the chip.

Here's what that looks like on a real chip — a close-up of a superconducting qubit's pads and microwave resonators. Each qubit couples to its own resonator, and the resonator's response is what actually gets measured, amplified, and digitized off-chip. The qubit's state is never read directly — it's inferred from how it perturbs a microwave signal passing through this structure.

Here's why the Josephson junction is non-negotiable. A plain capacitor and inductor wired together — an LC oscillator — has evenly spaced energy levels, like rungs on a ladder. Try to use the bottom two rungs as a qubit, and a pulse tuned to flip them would just as easily drive the next transition too, and the one after that. Swap the plain inductor for a Josephson junction, and the ladder's rungs become unevenly spaced. Now a pulse tuned precisely to the zero-to-one transition barely touches the one-to-two transition — which is exactly what makes the bottom two levels usable as an isolated, addressable qubit.

Every practical superconducting qubit design builds on this same core idea — one or more Josephson junctions providing the nonlinearity needed to carve a clean two-level system out of what would otherwise be useless. Next lesson: the transmon, the specific design that fixed an early noise problem and became the industry's default.
